extracted.intended_audience: general readers and students of planetary science / popular astronomy
extracted.subtask_description: A popular-science / textbook chapter arguing for vegetal interpretation of Mars’ dark areas and for a planetary history from terraqueous to terrestrial, using telescopic observations, comparative morphology, geology, and paleontology as evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seasonality requirement for vegetal interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: “For the change in question to be vegetal it must occur at the proper season of the planet’s year.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vegetal explanations must show timing consistent with seasonal growth/decay cycles. The chapter cites observations (e.g., Mare Erythraeum 1903 and 1905) where chromatic changes peak ~60–90 days after southern winter solstice, matching expectation for vegetation being at its deadest in winter. Repeated seasonal timing across oppositions strengthens vegetal interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recurrence across years as evidence of an annual phenomenon
rubrics_metrics.description: “From the recurrence of the phenomenon on two successive years, it is likely that it annually takes place.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the same chromatic metamorphosis appears in successive Martian years (examples: 1903 and 1905 occurrences of chocolate-brown in Mare Erythraeum), this supports an annual/seasonal process rather than a one-off event. Use multi-year records to assess regularity and rule out transient artifacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spatial progression (wave) of change indicates biological/regional process
rubrics_metrics.description: The observed differential timing between northern and southern portions of regions (tables of % blue-green depth) indicates a wave of returning growth coming from the north, not the south.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine separate subregions’ timelines (e.g., percentages in tables for northern vs southern Mare Erythraeum) to detect propagation direction; a coherent spatial-temporal wave supports a systematic planetary-seasonal cause (e.g., vegetation cycle) rather than random or observational error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Color-change character: tone fading vs new tint
rubrics_metrics.description: “Usually the change of hue seems essentially one of tone; the blue-green fades out... But there have been instances... where a quite new tint has surprisingly appeared.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate between mere tonal fading (suggesting overlay/removal of pigmentation or growth) and abrupt appearance of qualitatively new tints (e.g., chocolate-brown in 1903), which may indicate exposure of underlying substrate (fallow ground) or different processes. Use sequence of nightly/weekly observations to classify the change type.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogy to terrestrial fallow/desert colors as diagnostic evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: “Unlike the ochre of the light regions generally... the chocolate-brown precisely mimicked the complexion of fallow ground.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare Martian hues to terrestrial analogues (deserts, fallow fields, Painted Desert, Sahara) as supportive, not definitive, evidence. Note morphological and contextual corroboration is necessary because color alone can mislead; use analogies alongside seasonality and spatial patterning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absence of contradictory phenomena strengthens inference
rubrics_metrics.description: “But we need not to add example to example or proof to proof, for there are no phenomena that contradict it.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When building an interpretation (e.g., that blue-green areas are vegetation), explicitly check for and note any observations that would contradict the hypothesis. A lack of contradictory observations across diverse datasets increases confidence, but absence is not proof—still require positive corroboration (seasonality, propagation, recurrence).

rubrics_metrics.name: Morphology and relief (flatness / lower level on terminator) indicate former seas
rubrics_metrics.description: The dark regions “seem to lie below the level of the surface round about... when they pass over the terminator they invariably show as flattenings upon it, as if a slice of the surface had been pared off.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use terminator profiles and apparent flatness as morphological evidence that regions were ocean beds. Where a region appears depressed relative to surrounding corrugated terrain, interpret that as possible former water-covered basins; compare to lunar maria and Earth deep-sea floor morphology as analogues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparative planetology: cross-planet similarities as evidential support
rubrics_metrics.description: “Study of the several planets... reveals... the transition of its surface from a terraqueous to a purely terrestrial condition.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use similarities among bodies (Moon, Mars, Earth) — e.g., flat dark regions, levelness, volcanic cones around them — to infer shared evolutionary stages (loss of surface water). Comparative evidence is persuasive when morphological and stratigraphic parallels exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geologic stratigraphy as record of land reclaiming sea
rubrics_metrics.description: “Study of the earth’s surface reveals the preponderating encroachment of the land upon the sea since both began to be, and demonstrates that, except for local losses, the oceans have been contracting in size from archaic times. So much is evidenced by the successive places upon which marine beds have been laid down.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use stratigraphic records (marine beds, sedimentary sequences, mapped changes over geologic time) to document progressive emergence of land. Cite geological maps and syntheses (e.g., Dana’s work) showing temporal changes in continental extent as a model for planetary evolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paleontological succession as indicator of habitat shift
rubrics_metrics.description: “Fossil remains of the plants and creatures... show that the land has been steadily rising both in floral and faunal estimation... The record lies imprinted in the strata consecutively laid down.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret fossil assemblages across successive strata to infer increasing terrestrialization (appearance of land plants, insects, amphibians, reptiles, mammals). Use the sequence (Cambrian marine life → Silurian first land plants → Devonian primitive forests → Carboniferous amphibians → Permian reptiles → Mesozoic reptiles → Cenozoic mammals) as evidence for land becoming a dominant habitat.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical-mechanism explanations for water loss (internal absorption and atmospheric escape)
rubrics_metrics.description: “As the heat dissipates, the body begins to solidify... cracks... Into these the surface water seeps... Of the other means we know more... departure of the water in the form of gas, in consequence of the molecular motions.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate hypotheses about planetary desiccation by physical plausibility: (a) crustal cooling and increased permeability leading to internal sequestration of water, and (b) thermal/kinetic atmospheric escape of water vapor. Assess required temperature, age, and original atmosphere to estimate amounts lost; treat mechanism inference as contingent on physical parameters.
